newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL interbank rates rise as small houses borrow.
newsitem.headline: KL interbank rates rise as small houses borrow.

text.p: Interbank rates headed higher mainly on borrowings by small finance houses and merchant banks ahead of the weekend, dealers said.
But they said that the improving liquidity will limit the upside range of the rates.
"The rates are up across the board, about 20 points, as finances and merchants (houses) chase them up," said a money market dealer at a Malaysian bank. The lenders are led by foreign banks, he said.
The one-, two- and three-week money were at 7.50/70 percent against 7.40/50 previously, dealers said.
The one-month rate was at 7.50/60 percent versus 7.50, with the smaller houses having to pay up to 7.70 percent.
Three-month money was at 7.50/60 percent, unchanged, and the 12-month at 7.60/80 from 7.50/80.
Dealers said over the medium term, liquidity inflows will continue to depress the rates to its former levels.
At the 0300 GMT daily fixing on the Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates (Klibor), the average rates were all indicated lower.
The one-month average was 7.64 percent from 7.76 on Thursday, and both the three- and six-month at 7.75 against 7.79. The one-year average rate was quoted at 7.77 percent from 7.80.
Swap rates continued to inch steadily down to their former levels, though intermittent demand will cause gyrations, dealers said.
But longer-term swaps will remain supported as the Malaysian central bank continues to guard against spillover from ongoing problems of the Thai economy.
"There are fears that the Thai baht may be in trouble so the longer-end swaps will remain supported today," said market research firm I.D.E.A. in a report.
The one-month swap was quoted at 40/50 from 25/30 previusly.
Bank Negara Malaysia was expected to release the country's first quarter gross domestic product (GDP) data later today, which will give clues to interest rate direction.
Economists expect the GDP growth to be closely on either side of 8.0 percent, against 8.3 in the first quarter of 1996.
"I'll be happy if the numbers come out low, as there are still a lot of worries that the current account will worsen," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities.
